The two schools of Nature and Characteristics are like waves and water; they have never been separable from one another, yet their subsequent decline has led to such consequences.
Even going so far as to divide a river to drink from separate portions—how could this be the fault of Mañjuśrī or Maitreya?
Nor is it the intent of Aśvaghoṣa or Dharmapāla. To say that *tathatā* (suchness) undergoes perfuming is like saying that when the kalpa-fire blazes forth, empty space alone remains cold.
To say that *tathatā* does not undergo perfuming is like asking what remains of empty space when the kalpa-fire blazes forth.

Because it has often been seen to be corrupt, one knows that those who grasp the thread of its discourse will find both parts beautiful when combined, while those who lose its essential purport will find both parts flawed when separated.
Observe the fourth fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which says:

"For example, the substance of empty space is not composed of various phenomena, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various phenomena. With these words alone, two doubts are resolved like melting ice. This is excellent.
Now, the Great Master Zhi said: "To dogmatically cling to the principle that the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) alone gives rise to all phenomena—how does this differ from 'self-arising'?
To dogmatically cling to the view that the *ālayavijñāna* alone gives rise to all phenomena—how does this differ from 'other-arising'?

By analogy, even if one claims that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of the *dharmatā* and the *ālayavijñāna*, how does this differ from 'co-arising' (*sahaja*)? Even if one claims they are neither the *dharmatā* nor..."
If the Ālayavijñāna gives rise to all phenomena, how does this differ from arising without causes and conditions?

Viewed from this perspective, none of the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are free from being a form of slander. However, if one can skillfully penetrate the nature of non-arising and non-origination, then although the four propositions cannot be spoken of, they may nevertheless be spoken of due to the causes and conditions of the four *saṃtānas* (the fourfold purpose), namely, that which is called the inconceivable *tathatā*.

The perfuming that gives rise to all dharmas refers to the *ālayavijñāna* as the nature susceptible to perfuming; that which arises as all dharmas is entirely without anything that cannot [be so perfumed].
Thus I know that the Great Master Zhiwei truly awakened to the secret essentials of the provisional and the real;
therefore, even before the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* had arrived, he could anticipate its purport in such a manner. When this sūtra did arrive, the Great Master...

Those who study the Tiantai school cannot help but be obscured by the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), while those who study the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) remain deluded regarding the perfect principle (*yuanli*).
Thus, various interpretations proliferate, and all lose the essential framework. To investigate where the principles and meanings ultimately converge is much like a mosquito biting an iron spike;
to judge the placement of characters is like boring a hole only to plant a mustache there—before the dawn has even broken.
On the very day I shaved my head, I began to study this scripture; however, every time I consulted the old commentaries, I was frequently bewildered and distressed.

It was only after practicing seated meditation at Shuangjing that I first broke free from the shackles of literal words. Furthermore, through several rounds of expounding upon its profound principles, I severed the roots of conceptual entanglement.
By investigating both schools and fusing them within the mirror of the mind, it was only upon reaching Wénlǐng to propagate the Dharma that I finally attained [true understanding].

I took up my brush and wrote swiftly; before long, the draft was completed and the carving finished. The woodblocks remained at the Gandhamādana Precept Platform and could not be carried beyond the Yangtze River.
Now, while my illusory journey through Pude Temple briefly revealed these private matters, my friends pursued me relentlessly.
Master Dun conceived the idea to reprint them, so I have composed these few words as a preface to open up the past for all eternity.
To breach the fences that have not yet been broken and to violate the prohibitions long strictly established is to speak from a low station with high pretensions;
how can one escape blame? Nevertheless, among those gentlemen who have transcended the world, it is surely understood that one does not reject words because of the person who speaks them.

The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is the principle-substance (*dharmatā*) of the mind’s own nature (*svabhāva*).
It remains unchanging while following conditions, thereby integrating the four categories (*catuḥskandha*) as nothing but this fundamental reality;

it remains wondrously unchanging while following conditions, thereby permeating each of the seven elements (*saptamahābhūta*) throughout the Dharma-realm. It is like ice [which is essentially water]. Revised by the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Wēnlíng Dàofǎng.

The beginning and end of water is nothing other than its nature of moisture; it is like the myriad phenomena of the great void that do not reject one another. Thus, the ten realms are manifested from the single mind.
Through the "actualization" (shizao) and the "inherent potentiality" (ligu), all is universally encompassed and contained within a single realm and the three truths.

Whether distinguished horizontally or traversed vertically, these are neither identical nor separate. Based upon this, one accomplishes the causes and effects of self-cultivation; therefore, it is called the "Secret Cause of the Tathāgata."

The cultivation and realization of the definitive meaning (nītārtha) is precisely this; because it constitutes the cause and effect for transforming others, it is called the "Wondrous Cultivation of the Cause and Effect of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, the Śūraṅgama. This [cultivation] fully returns to the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). How could the power of function for transforming others be separated from the essence and the principle? When the two texts clarify the distinction between substance and function, the golden sand establishes the discernment; when the two meanings are resolved, the flowered mansion has its gate. Having faith that the skillful means are none other than the nature of the sages, and having selected the faculty of the ear as uniquely sharp, one follows these clear instructions with earnest diligence, where both precepts and vehicle are urgent.
The site of practice is established, with the Exoteric and Esoteric mutually supporting;
without gradual stages, one establishes gradual stages, and while manifesting the primary and auxiliary practices through successive levels, one realizes that these very levels are no levels at all.

The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) one undergoes is like a phantom; the thorough investigation of the seven realms of existence reveals they arise solely from delusion regarding this Great Buddha-Crown Principle, whereby one falsely undergoes saṃsāra.
Who could fail to realize that these flowers in the sky have no separate substance?

By carefully discerning the five māras, one seeks to awaken to this Great Buddha-Crown Principle, yet midway one may fall into confusion. Who knows that the root and source of these false thoughts is truly this very principle?
It is the essence of the teachings for this one lifetime, the secret key to becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch, the ultimate goal of the unsurpassed Perfect and Sudden teaching,
the expedient means that universally benefits those of the three capacities, the extraordinary Dharma gate that transcends the provisional and the Small Vehicle,
and the true seal of the Real Mark that destroys demons and heretics. Therefore, it reveals to people in a single thought how to extinguish karmic obstructions, like turning over a great...
The patriarchs relied on the teachings to practice the Way and attain Bodhi, as clearly as observing fruit in the palm of one's hand;

Master Zhiyi paid homage from afar upon hearing the name alone, undaunted by the labor involved, and Venerable Prajñāruci cut his own arm to transmit the text from afar, not shrinking from the suffering.

I, Zhixu, having been born in this age of Semblance Dharma, have fortunately encountered these magnificent expositions; were it not for the divine power of these Great Beings, how could I have gained even a taste of them? It is truly extraordinary.

The phrasing is perfect and the meaning is subtle; the purport is far-reaching and the intent profound. Although commentaries and sub-commentaries are numerous, the ultimate truth has not yet been established.
Lamenting that the definitive meaning remains hidden and grieving that no one tells those lost at the ford of delusion, I do not decline my own meager learning but instead exhaust my limited clarity.

Having gathered the strengths of many and reconciled them into a single principle, I have refined my studies and exhausted my thoughts to restate this profound text, not daring to compete with what came before.
People suffer from merely comparing right and wrong; they should instead seek the underlying connections within this sutra deeply for themselves.

I wish that my fellow practitioners will examine it with an open mind and keen insight, and there will surely be those who understand its similarities and differences, its depth and shallowness, its contradictions and harmonies, and its gains and losses.
This preface was composed on the twenty-seventh day of the third month of the spring in the Jīmō year of the Chóngzhēn era.

To explain the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*) of this sutra: first, the explanation of the title; second, the manifestation of the essence (*tattva*); third, the clarification of the primary purpose (*mūla-artha*); fourth, the discernment of its function (*kāritra*);
and fifth, the analysis of the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding these five aspects, there are both general and specific explanations.

The general explanation of the seven sections is fully detailed in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) and will not be repeated here. Now, within the specific explanation, the explanation of the title has two parts: first, [the explanation] based on the sutra itself.

Regarding the five titles established [in this scripture], which clarify the principles of inclusion and abbreviation, I shall now provide a formal explanation of the general and specific characters in the current title.

First, concerning the clarification of inclusion and abbreviation: according to the text of the Sūtra where the Buddha answers Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the name, there are five phrases in total. The first states:
"The name of this Sūtra is the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Sitātapatra Unsurpassed Jewel Seal of the Ten Directions."
The Tathāgata’s pure ocean-eye now remains as only three characters, with eighteen characters omitted;
the three characters "Dafoding" (Great Buddha-Crown) fully reveal the true essence of this sutra.

Therefore, these characters must be preserved, for they are both the basis upon which the perfect teachings of Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism rely and that which is revealed by those very teachings. *Siddhārthapāṇḍaravāsinī*.

The Unsurpassed Jewel Seal of Lokeśvara (Luo Wushang Baoyin) is the esoteric exposition that does not depart from this essence; the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions is the exoteric exposition that does not depart from this essence.
Thus, by preserving these three characters alone, the essence of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings is fully encompassed without omission.
Second, it is also called "Saving and Protecting One's Own Causes," which delivers and liberates Ānanda and others.
In this assembly, the bhikṣuṇī Śrāvakī has attained bodhicitta and entered the ocean of universal knowledge;

her name is abbreviated for the sake of brevity, as it is established solely from its function, being both proximate and narrow. The two individuals—Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī Śrāvakī—can be subsumed within the category of all bodhisattvas;
the two dharmas of bodhi and universal knowledge can be subsumed within the *Śūraṅgama*.
This is because the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is that which enables one to attain and enter the ocean of universal knowledge of the bodhicitta, while that which is attained and entered is the ocean itself;
since the subject and object are fundamentally non-dual, this is so. Third, it is also called "The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization";
this name is preserved in its entirety because it constitutes the essential core of this sutra. Fourth, it is also called...

The *Dafangguang Miaolianhuawang Shifangfumuduanluozhou* (The Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions Dhāraṇī Mantra) also establishes its title based on its essence and its central tenet;

as it is a concise expression of the esoteric meaning, both [the essence and tenet] are abbreviated. In reality, however, it is simply the meaning of the "Secret Cause of the Tathāgata" from the *Great Buddha-Topknot*.
Since the exoteric and esoteric teachings fundamentally possess no two essences and no two tenets, it is possible to [treat them as one].
The fifth way of subsuming the esoteric within the exoteric is as follows: the twelve characters "Also named the Mantra-Phrases of Empowerment; the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas;
Śūraṃgama" establish their name based on their function. By omitting four characters and retaining eight, this too is a case of subsuming the esoteric within the exoteric.
Next, the formal explanation is divided into two parts: first, a combined explanation of the general and specific aspects; second, a detailed explanation of each phrase.
Regarding the first, the combined explanation: all sutras possess both general and specific names.

Since teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*caryā*), and principle (*tattva*) all involve general and specific aspects, the nineteen characters beginning with "Great Buddha-Usnīṣa" constitute a specific teaching because their names differ from those of other scriptures.

Because they share the same name, "Sūtra," the teachings are common; because practice arises based on these teachings, practices differ, ranging from one to the infinite, and thus practices are distinct.
Because they converge upon the same ultimate reality, practices are common. Although the principle is nameless, names serve as its gateways;

the principle follows the gates, for through the four teachings and sixteen gates, one enters the principle. Thus, while the principle is one, the gates are distinct, as the gates follow [the principle].
Because the principle entered through one gate is precisely the principle of all gates, and the principle entered through all gates is precisely the principle of one gate, the principle is pervasive.
This first discusses the pervasive and the particular based on a single transformation; next, it discusses them based on a single sūtra:

because the various preceding and following passages have different expressive characteristics, the teaching is distinct; yet because the principle expressed is one, the teaching is pervasive. These two aspects constitute the distinction between the particular and the pervasive.
The fifteen holy skillful means differ in their approaches because they are many gates; yet they are identical in their realization because they all lead to perfect penetration.

Thus, while the approaches differ, the penetration is universal. Each of the twenty-five gates fully embodies the entire principle; thus, while the principles appear distinct, each single gate completely integrates and encompasses all other gates.

Thus, while the principles appear distinct, their integration is universal. Furthermore, regarding a single title: "Great Buddha-Crown" refers to the principle; "Ultimate Meaning" refers to the teaching; and "Śūraṅgama" refers to the practice.

These are all partial citations intended to provide what is essential for a complete treatise to correspond with the words of the sūtras; they possess both general and specific meanings as they arise spontaneously.

Furthermore, regarding the term "Great" (*mahā*) mentioned in a single character, the Sanskrit *mahā* contains three meanings: namely, great, many, and superior. "Great" refers to the principle (*tattva*);
"many" refers to practice (*caryā*); and "superior" refers to the teaching (*śāsana*). Moreover, because the principle is great, the teaching and practice are likewise so.
Because the great practices are manifold, the teachings and principles are likewise manifold; because the teachings are supreme, the principles and practices are also supreme.

Within a single character there are immeasurable meanings, and within each of those meanings the meanings are again immeasurable—how much more so for a single phrase, a single title, a single sutra, and all the sutras?
This concludes the combined explanation of the general and specific aspects.
Next, the text is divided and explained in two parts: first, the explanation of the specific name consisting of nineteen characters;

second, the explanation of the general name "Sūtra. The explanation of the specific name is further divided into two parts: first, the selection and determination; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the selection and determination:
the specific names of all sūtras are immeasurable, yet if one summarizes them, they do not exceed seven types: first, single dharmas; second... [text continues].

The single person, the three single metaphors, the four persons, the five dharmas, the six persons, and the seven persons—each with their respective dharmas and metaphors—are now presented in this sutra primarily by way of persons and dharmas, briefly incorporating metaphors as well.
Thus, the dharmas have both nature (*prakṛti*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*); persons have both cause (*hetu*) and fruit (*phala*).
The Great Buddha-Topknot is the dharma of nature; it is the definitive meaning of the secret cause for cultivation and realization, and the foremost among the myriad practices.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* practice is the fruit-stage of the Tathāgata, while the various Bodhisattvas are those on the causal stage. To briefly include its symbolic meaning:

the manifestation of the Buddha’s crown represents the inherent nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) possessed by all sentient beings. Therefore, when explained through explicit terminology, it is called the *Mahā-buddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra*;
when explained through secret terminology, it is called the *Mahā-buddhoṣṇīṣa Mantra*. It is named according to that which is symbolized, and may also be so designated.

This serves as an analogy. The formal explanation is divided into two parts: first, the detailed explanation of each phrase; second, a comprehensive discussion of the general outline. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the explanation of the Great Buddha-Crown;
second, the explanation of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning; and third, the explanation of the various Bodhisattvas.
The Universal Practice of the Śūraṅgama. First, the explanation of the Great Buddha-Crown is further divided into three parts:
first, a brief explanation based on the dharma of mind; second, an extensive explanation based on the dharma of Buddha; and third, an analogical explanation based on the dharma of sentient beings.
Now, the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are without distinction; this nature of non-distinction is precisely the nature of the Great Buddha-Crown. This rational nature resides in...
Delusion does not decrease, and awakening does not increase; the single nature is all natures, and all natures are the single nature.
To explain this according to each interpretation, a single dharma is universally able to penetrate all dharmas. Why must these three interpretations be made?

It is specifically because the nature-virtue (prakṛti-guṇa) exists within the bonds of affliction such that no one can comprehend it—just as who could know a treasure in a dark room? Therefore, one must rely on the Buddha.
The three virtues of the realms clarify their ultimate aim, yet those who are ignorant still claim that ability belongs exclusively to the Buddha;

therefore, one must further examine the identity [of all things] by means of the nine realms and the three natures. When the ten realms are presented together, both principle and phenomena are entirely equal;

yet, even so, if one does not realize that the two layers of the three thousand worlds coexist within a single thought-moment, one will doubt that the dharmas of sentient beings are as vast as the dharmas of the Buddha.
Because this work is profound, it must necessarily rely on the three causes within a single thought-moment to identify its essentials.
If one understands that there is no distinction between mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, then every word reveals the ultimate truth and every phrase makes known the fundamental source.

For those who do not yet understand, I have provided these three rounds of explanation; furthermore, fearing that many might become mired in mere words or attached to the literal expression—like those who talk of food without eating or count jewels without possessing them—I have written this.
Now, first providing a brief guide from the immediate and essential perspective so that one may enter contemplation according to the text:

regarding the initial brief explanation based on the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), these three characters "Great Buddha-Peak" (*Mahā-buddha-uṣṇīṣa*) directly point to the present nature of the mind of sentient beings, fully manifesting the fundamental principle (*tattva*) discussed throughout this entire scripture.
For the single thought-moment of our own present experience is truly without boundaries and without—

In its spatial dimensions, it has no beginning or end, nor does it exist within temporal kalpas; vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, its very substance is absolute and beyond conceptualization—therefore, it is called "Great.
The Sūtra says: "The essence of all causes and effects, and even the finest dust motes of the world, are formed by the mind.
It also says: "That which is unchanging is fundamentally without birth or extinction. And it says: "That which does not return to you is not..."
"Who are you? and so forth, up to "The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect;

its clarity and perfection mean that awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous"—all these passages directly point to this very present thought-moment as being, in its own essence, eternally pervasive, lacking nothing and having no excess.
It is like the bright moon seen in a single instant: it is the very same moon that has existed from the beginningless past to the endless future; one cannot say it is merely "this" moon.

Furthermore, just as a single reflection of the moon in water cannot be called a partial moon, for it is the entire body of the moon in the sky, so too our present moment-to-moment awareness—this clear and constant knowing that must not be allowed to grow dim—is named "Buddha.
"Buddha" means "awakened. As the Sūtra says: "Seeing thus..."
The nature [of seeing] belongs to the mind, not the eye; you should know that the natures of hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognition are likewise so.
Furthermore, it is said: "When the head moves and shakes, seeing has no movement; when the hands open and close, seeing has no expansion or contraction.

It is also said: "To perceive what is perceived is a cataract; perception itself is not within the cataract. And: "If you say that hearing is real while saying there is nothing, who knows that there is nothing? This extends even to its physical form.
"Though one sleeps, the nature of hearing does not become darkened; even if your physical form were to dissolve and your life-force were to depart, how could this nature be extinguished by you?
All such statements reveal the awakened nature of the single thought-moment of the present.
This nature of the single thought-moment of our own present cannot be traced, cannot be described, is free from faults, transcends all negation, and its function is inexhaustible.

Reaching the ultimate nobility and the pinnacle of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one does not fall into any numerical categories; therefore, it is called the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). It is like the crown of a Buddha’s head:
although it is a wondrous mark (*lakṣaṇa*), it cannot be seen. As the Sūtra says: "Where now are the mind and the eyes?

And again: "By what is the mind constituted? When my fist shines forth, [the mind is not found]. Therefore, in the seven locations there is no sign or perception; as it is not a substantial entity, it cannot be apprehended.
The finger cannot be pointed at; it is neither light nor darkness, nor form nor emptiness, nor is it sensation, hearing, cognition, or perception.
All of these serve to reveal that this present single thought-moment is fundamentally free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Traditionally, commentators have interpreted these three characters either by focusing solely on the Dharma, asserting that "this Dharma is the supreme crest-ornament of Great Enlightenment," or...
"Taking it solely from the perspective of analogy" means using the Buddha’s crown as a metaphor so that one does not become stuck in views or signs.
"Taking it solely from the perspective of phenomena" means that because the transformation Buddhas within the Tathāgata’s crown preach the mantra, it receives the name "Great Buddha-Crown.

"Taking it solely from the perspective of principle" means that "Great" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "Buddha" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), and "Crown" refers to liberation (*vimukti*). It is like carrying a wooden board: each [term] represents one aspect.
If one perceives a single aspect and knows it as a complete analogy, it reveals the entirety of the Dharma and expresses the full meaning of the principle;

thus, the various explanations converge upon these two meanings. Indeed, the transformation Buddha appearing from within the crown of the Tathāgata’s head is also called the "unconditioned mind-Buddha," which precisely symbolizes the inherent nature-virtue possessed by all sentient beings.
This inherent nature-virtue is fundamentally most noble and majestic, like a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).
In the king’s dream, although he was transformed into an ant—deluded, inverted, and seeking the scent down the steps—the body upon the bed remained exactly as it was before.
Furthermore, this nature-virtue (prakṛti-guṇa) is neither characterized by form nor devoid of form;

it is like the crown of the Buddha’s head (*uṣṇīṣa*), which, though invisible, is not non-existent. That it is not non-existent is precisely the meaning of "not empty" in its ultimate reality (*tathatā*).

Because it can emit radiant light from the crown of the head and manifest transformations that are invisible—this being the meaning of emptiness as it truly is—it is able to transcend all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
It is free from both "is" and "is not," and from the meanings of "empty" and "not empty. While appearing to have two distinct natures, in reality there are no two;
this is the meaning of the non-dual, perfect fusion of emptiness and non-emptiness. Therefore, it is neither negation nor illumination, for negation and illumination are identical.
At that time, it is thus: not departing from a single analogy, the three dharmas are manifest. Because the *dharmakāya* is great, there is nothing it does not encompass;
because *prajñā* is great, there is nothing it does not illuminate; because *vimukti* is great, there is nothing it does not harmonize.

Because one awakens to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the one is empty and all is empty; because one awakens to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the one is provisional and all is provisional. Because one awakens to...

Because the Middle Truth is such that one is all-middle and emptiness is all-emptiness, and because emptiness lacks the characteristic of emptiness, there is not a single dharma that transcends emptiness.
Because one is all-false and falsity lacks the characteristic of falsity, there is not a single dharma that transcends falsity.
Because one is all-middle and the middle lacks the characteristic of the middle, there is not a single... [dharma that transcends the middle].
The Dharma transcends these three characters; together they manifest the three virtues, yet they are not sequential. Each single character possesses the three meanings, yet they are not horizontal.

Being neither vertical nor horizontal, it is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*). The beings of the seven destinies are deluded by this and sink into saṃsāra, yet their delusion does not diminish it.
The followers of the two vehicles are obscured by this and become withered and silent, yet their obscuration does not decrease it. The Tathāgata realizes this.
The fruit of the ultimate fruition is also not a fruit; the Bodhisattva realizes this as the true cause, yet the cause is also not a cause.
One who reads the scriptures well can recognize their own mind within these three characters, and thus the Unsurpassed Jewel King arrives of its own accord without being sought.
One who skillfully contemplates the mind can recognize this wondrous principle within a single moment of thought.
Because the boundless treasury of Dharma is clearly illuminated in every sphere of contact, it was first briefly explained in terms of the mental dharmas.
Next, regarding the extensive explanation in terms of the Buddha-dharmas: since the mental dharmas are perfectly complete, what is there that they do not encompass?

If one is deluded and stubbornly ignorant, one should further contemplate the fruit-deeds; by verifying the fruit, one knows the cause, thereby enabling oneself to realize and attain them. What is called "extensive" does not exceed this extensiveness.

This summary does not mean that there is any further Buddha-dharma outside of the mind. Furthermore, it is explained through four intentions: first, an explanation based on phenomena (*dharma*); second, an explanation based on principle (*li*);

third, an explanation based on the teachings (*dharma*); and fourth, an explanation based on analogies (*upamā*). Although these appear to employ ancient interpretations universally, there are two points of difference from them:
first, if one were merely to employ ancient interpretations universally, they could not be mutually integrated; [only] with these four explanations can they be harmonized.

Although these two versions are presented separately, their meanings are in fact harmonious. Regarding the four explanations provided here, while the terminology is identical to that of the ancient [commentaries], the flavor of the meaning is vastly different;
readers should examine this for themselves. First, the explanation based on phenomena (*dharma*):
the first fascicle of the Sūtra states, "The World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness; within that light, thousand-petaled lotuses were produced."
In the seventh fascicle of the *Ratnapadma-buddhāvatamsaka-nirmāṇa-kāya-samādhi-dhyāna-prabhāsa-mantra-sūtra*, it is said:

"This is the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown (*anavalokitamūrdha-lakṣaṇa*), the unconditioned mind-Buddha. Radiance issues forth from his crown as he sits upon a precious lotus flower, proclaiming this Heart Mantra.
It further states: "From within the uṣṇīṣa of the World-Honored One, hundreds of jewel lights surge forth, and so on, until they manifest..."
From the Buddha’s crown, ten rays of light composed of a hundred jewels were emitted;

each ray of light universally manifested ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges] of Vajrapāṇis, Secret Traces, who held mountains and wielded clubs, pervading the entire realm of empty space. Thereafter, he proclaimed the divine mantra.
It is further said that this mantra is also called the "Tathāgata’s Crown," while the title of the scripture itself is simply stated as such.
It is named the "Great Uṣṇīṣa-Śītata-Pāṇḍarā Unsurpassed Jewel Seal," for it is the pure ocean-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Thus, one may provide a direct explanation based on the phenomenal aspect (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*):

since this mantra is the Great Uṣṇīṣa mantra, this sutra is titled the *Mahā-uṣṇīṣa Sūtra*. Now, a dharma-gate concerning phenomenal characteristics must necessarily have that which it symbolizes; and as for this—
Divine Spell: Why does Śākyamuni not proclaim [the truth] himself, but instead manifests a transformation Buddha from the light at his crown?
Furthermore, for what reason is this transformation Buddha called the "Unconditioned Mind Buddha"?

It is because when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni had already manifested leaving home to cultivate the Way and was about to realize Bodhi, sentient beings, having become accustomed to seeing him, believed he was born from his father and mother as a physical body.
Through cultivation and realization, one attains the fruit, yet this remains distinct from our own condition; for we fail to realize that their mind-nature is equal.

Thus, the manifestation of a transformation Buddha upon the crown of the head signifies that this state does not belong to the realm of conditioned accomplishment, but is rather the very nature of the mind itself—the unconditioned *dharmakāya*, the naturally wondrous, perfectly enlightened, supreme, and foremost source of all response and transformation.
Because it is the body, it is called "Great"; because it is wondrous enlightenment, it is called "Buddha"; because it is most honored and supreme, it is called the "Crown.
This Great Buddha-Crown is simply the source of the mind, which is equally possessed by the ten realms.

Recently, there have been interpreters who, upon seeing that transformation-buddhas emanate from the light on the crown in the sutra text, wished to take the five characters "Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata" as a single phrase; this is clearly a forced and fragmented reading of the text.
The three characters "Zhi-bu-zhi" (The Essential Meaning is Not Known) are already sufficient to encompass the matters concerning the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha. Question:

Since it is said that these represent the Dharma (*dharmaparyāya*), why do they not overlap with the subsequent section which explains according to principle (*li*)? Answer: That [subsequent section] directly explains the principles of the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), whereas this merely relies on phenomena (*vastu*) to represent the Dharma;
thus, it still belongs to the explanation of phenomena (*vastuvyākhyā*). Question: Since there is something represented here, why does it not overlap with the following?
The lower section answers by means of an analogy: that [previous] analogy of expanding one's vision so as not to be obstructed by signs has no bearing on the actual matter;

whereas the present case involves a definitive expression regarding the facts themselves, and is therefore analogous to the various events described in the sutras—such as the emission of light and the shaking of the earth—and is not analogous to metaphors such as ice and water or the layered handkerchief. Second, the explanation according to principle states: the ancients said...

To claim that "Great" (*mahā*) corresponds to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "Buddha" (*buddha*) to Prajñā, and "Crown" (*śikhin*) to Liberation (*vimukti*)—assigning these three characters to these meanings separately—may indeed be so;

however, this would fragment the text. Furthermore, the principle of the three perfect virtues (*triguṇa*) is utterly beyond being either vertical or horizontal. To treat them as a single path would never exhaust their true meaning.
Here, I clarify that the three characters "Great," "Buddha," and "Crown" directly expound the three virtues on the level of fruition, with each character [representing one].
The three meanings of "perfectly endowed" (*paripūrṇa*) are likewise not horizontal; that which is called "Great" praises the three virtues:

the Greatness of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Greatness of the marks of Prajñā, and the Greatness of the function of liberation (*vimukti*). That which is called "Buddha" designates these three virtues:

the Dharma-body is original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*), Prajñā is initial enlightenment (*ādi-avabodha*), and liberation is ultimate enlightenment (*niṣṭhā-avabodha*). Furthermore, Prajñā is self-enlightenment (*svasaṃvedana-avabodha*) and liberation is awakening [for others].
His Dharma-body is fully awakened; that which is called the "Crown" (*uṣṇīṣa*) signifies the ultimate consummation of the three virtues.
The Dharma-body has nothing further above it, Prajñā cannot be seen as a form, and Liberation emits light and manifests transformations;
therefore, these are combined and named the Great Buddha-Crown (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*). Furthermore, the three meanings contained within this single word each, in turn, perfectly embody the three [virtues].
Regarding the three meanings of the term "Great" (*mahā*): first, "great" refers to the *dharmakāya*, as it encompasses all phenomena; as the Sūtra says:
"This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. Second, "great" refers to *prajñā*, as it illumines all objects; as the Sūtra says:
"I, by means of wondrous clarity that neither perishes nor arises... [and so forth]. Third, "great" refers to the supreme (*parama*). These are the three meanings generally expressed.
The convergence of the *tathāgatagarbha* and so forth, wherein one becomes immeasurable and so on, constitutes this supreme liberation because it transcends all things;
as the sutra says: "If one can transform objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata.
Thus, the *dharmakāya* is both manifold and supreme, *prajñā* is both supreme and great, and liberation is both great and manifold. As for the manifoldness of the *dharmakāya*, it is pervasive.
The *Sarvatrānupamadharmakāyasūtra* states: "The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true nature of *tathatā*.
To mention any single aggregate, any single faculty, any single particle, or any single consciousness is to encounter the entire body of the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is not merely a partial portion. It is like ten thousand people looking up at the full moon, each seeing its entire form. If each [person]...
Just as the full moon follows along with each person’s various views, so too it is with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*): though it is neither one nor many, it is spoken of as being many.
Since the supreme Dharma-body is called the "ever-abiding true mind" and the "essence of pure luminosity," how could it not be the most supreme?
This is easily understood. As for the supremacy of Prajñā, it is because it is the foremost *pāramitā*.
The Greatness of Prajñā (Wisdom) due to the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision: Because it is non-dual in essence with suchness and reality, as the Sūtra says:
"Only the wondrous, enlightened clarity universally illumines the Dharma-realm," and so forth. The Greatness of Liberation:

Because inconceivable liberation is, in its very substance, free from all dependence and opposition, as the Sūtra says: "The deluded mind suddenly ceases; this cessation is itself Bodhi, the supreme, pure, and luminous."
The mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm; "many liberations" refers to the fact that every dharma is without bondage.

This is like the hundred phrases on liberation in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, or the thirty-two gates in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, or the twenty-five perfect penetrations (*yuan-tong*) in this sutra.
Regarding the three meanings of the word "Buddha": it is the awakening of oneself, the awakening of others, and the fulfillment of awakening. To speak briefly, "awakening of oneself" is...
Prajñā (wisdom) awakening others is the awakening of liberation; its fulfillment is the Dharma-body. Thus, self-awakening is the realization of the three virtues within oneself;
awakening others is causing them also to realize the three virtues; and the fulfillment of awakening is the non-duality of self and others.
Furthermore, original awakening is the three virtues within the nature (*dharmatā*), while initial awakening is [the three virtues] within the causal stage.
The ultimate awakening of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) is precisely the three meanings of the syllable *Tiṃ* within the fruit [of Buddhahood]. These three meanings are:
the meaning of supreme honor, the meaning of invisibility, and the meaning of emitting light and manifesting transformations. To speak briefly:

supreme honor is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), invisibility is Prajñā, and emitting light and manifesting transformations is liberation (*vimukti*). Nevertheless, there is nothing among these three virtues that is not supreme.
The three honored virtues are simultaneously invisible, yet that which manifests and that which is manifested—each and every one—is none other than the entire substance of the three virtues.
Thus, both the words and their meaning are sublime; the secret treasury is profoundly serene. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally a wondrous, perfect, and complete mind; it is neither mind nor emptiness, neither earth, water, wind, nor fire, and it is not the six sense organs."
The six sense objects are not it; the six consciousness realms are not it; the twelve links of dependent origination are not it;
the wisdom attained through the Four Noble Truths is not it; the perfection of the Six Paramitas is not it; the three titles of the Tathāgata are not it; and the four virtues of Nirvana are not it.

Because all these—both mundane and supramundane—are "not," it is the Tathāgatagarbha, the primordial luminosity and wondrous mind. It is the mind itself, and it is emptiness, and so on, even unto "itself" and "purity."

Because this is both the mundane and the supramundane, it is the wondrously luminous fundamental mind of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is neither identical nor different, and neither identical nor non-identical.
You should know that this "identity" is the ultimate realization of the Dharma of the Great Uṣṇīṣa.
For this Tathāgatagarbha-mind is simply the fundamental principle-body inherently possessed by all sentient beings; it is only through the Buddha’s wondrous luminosity that...

Because of the convergence of cessation and non-arising, one gives rise to the wondrously enlightened nature of true thusness (*tathatā*). This so-called "arising" means to attain what is originally possessed;

there is truly nothing newly acquired. Furthermore, it should be understood that this very mind of the Tathāgata-garbha, which is inherently complete, does not mean that there exists some separate, universal dharma-gate outside of the provisional designations of the ten realms of existence and their environments and inhabitants, serving as the agent of realization.

It is not that the subject (the capacity to perceive) is identical to the simultaneous negation and illumination, nor that the objects (the ten realms of phenomena) are identical to the simultaneous negation and illumination;
rather, it is because the unchanging nature blazes forth as it follows conditions, and while following conditions, its entire essence remains unchanging.
Therefore, within the ten dharma-realms—whether defiled or pure, whether substantial or nominal, whether the environment or the inhabitants—[it is thus].
If one correctly grasps any single dharma, it is the entire body of the Tathāgatagarbha mind;
it is simultaneously neither-identical-nor-different, both negated and both illuminated, perfectly interfused in accordance with the nature, and inconceivable.

To grasp any single dharma while all ten realms are simultaneously detached—where detachment is non-detachment and non-detachment is detachment—is, for the time being, the primary meaning. Following...
To take up a single dharma and find that the ten realms are all "neither" is, for the time being, the meaning of *buddha* (the Awakened One).
To take up any single dharma and find that the ten realms are all "identical" is, for the time being, the meaning of *mūrdhan* (the Summit).

Furthermore, to be neither identical nor non-identical, and yet both identical and non-identical, is the meaning of the "Greatness of Essence," the meaning of "Original Awakening," and the meaning of "Supreme Honored One. [In this state,] the ten realms are all...
"Non-being" refers to the meaning of the greatness of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-mahātva*), the meaning of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), and the meaning of being invisible.

"The ten realms are all identical" refers to the meaning of the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahātva*), the meaning of ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*), and the meaning of manifest transformation.

One should reflect accordingly that even within a single meaning, these three meanings are once again perfectly complete. Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha-mind is fundamentally detached from [all phenomena].
"Being identical yet detached" means that identity and non-identity, negation and illumination, occur simultaneously and are inconceivable.
Specifically, because the unchanging is identical with following conditions, all things are "neither"; because the unchanging is identical with following conditions, all things are "both.
Furthermore, "the unchanging following conditions" refers to this single essence possessing three meanings, which universally follow the delusions of the ten realms.
To realize that the various conditions of defilement and purity remain unchanging amidst those conditions means to point directly to the fact that all phenomena— whether deluded or awakened,
defiled or pure— within the ten realms are, without exception, identical to this single essence. Therefore,

the fact that "all are simultaneously non-existent" is termed the meaning of "emptiness as it truly is," while the fact that "all are simultaneously existent" is termed the meaning of "non-emptiness as it truly is."
Emptiness and non-emptiness are merely the two meanings naturally and perfectly endowed within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
yet its essence is fundamentally neither empty nor non-empty. Therefore, it can simultaneously illumine both emptiness and non-emptiness.
Thus, the sutras refer only to the Tathāgatagarbha as the "fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind," the "originally luminous mind," and the "wondrously luminous mind. Fundamentally, there are no three.
The name "Tathāgatagarbha" was first posed as a question by Ānanda and subsequently described by Avalokiteśvara;

in both instances, it is referred to solely as the "empty Tathāgatagarbha," with no mention of two other names—namely, the "non-empty Tathāgatagarbha" or the "both-empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Later generations have failed to directly clarify that the mind of the Tathāgatagarbha possesses these three meanings.
Thus, three names are established in distinct clarity, causing those who rely on words and cling to phrases to mistakenly believe that each of the Three Baskets possesses a separate essence;
this is indeed lamentable. Having concluded the explanation according to principle, the third is the explanation according to the Dharma:
this is the samādhi in which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas themselves abide; therefore, it is called the most honored and unsurpassed.
It is called the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; it is also named the First Noble Truth; it is also named the True Ultimate Meaning within the Ultimate Meaning;
it is also named the Unsurpassed Path of Awakening; it is also named the Dharma Free from Conceptual Proliferation;
it is also named Abhidharma; it is also named the Truly Perfect Penetration; and it is also named the Peerless Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
To summarize the essential point of focusing the mind: it is simply that the fundamental nature of the sentient being’s mind is eternally unchanging, yet it accords with conditions;
while it accords with conditions, it does not change. To be deluded by it is to undergo boundless birth and death, like the frantic running of Yajñadatta;
to awaken to it is to realize that nirvana is inherently present, like the divine pearl that was originally there all along. Only this principle is the truth.

Because it is the reality, it is the supreme crest-dharma of the Great Awakened One. In the sutra, first, precious light surges forth from the *svastika* on his chest and universally bathes the crowns of the heads of all Tathāgatas in the ten directions;
next, the light from the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas in the ten directions comes to bathe the Buddha’s crown.
This continues until the teaching on the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*) is concluded, at which point the five limbs of the World-Honored One and the Buddhas of the ten directions [are joined].
Simultaneously, they emitted jewel-like radiance that mutually drenched the crowns of the Buddhas and all the Bodhisattvas; this signifies the most supreme Dharma:
namely, teaching based on the most supreme principle, practice arising from the most supreme teaching, and returning to accord with this most supreme principle through practice.
Teaching, principle, and practice—these three are all termed the "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. Fourth, in terms of...
Regarding the metaphor: the old explanation says, "to use the Buddha’s crown as a metaphor so that one does not become stuck in appearances.
This means that although the Buddha’s crown is a form, because it cannot be seen, one does not become stuck in form; this is merely the meaning of what is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"If one sees all forms as non-form, then one sees the Tathāgata. However, if one employs it skillfully, it becomes [the realization of the Middle Way].
Those who do not properly understand the initial gateway of the Mahayana teachings still fall into the trap of signlessness (*animitta*). The Prajñāpāramitā is like a great mass of fire;
it cannot be touched from any side, for to touch it is to be burned. How can one interpret it solely through the meaning of signlessness?
I now say that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha cannot be illustrated by means of having signs (*sanimitta*), nor can it be illustrated by means of being signless (*animitta*).
It cannot be illustrated by the characteristic of both existence and non-existence, nor can it be illustrated by the characteristic of neither existence nor non-existence.
For example, the crown of the Buddha’s head cannot be said to have characteristics, nor can it be said to be without characteristics;

it cannot be said to have the characteristic of both existence and non-existence, nor can it be said to have the characteristic of neither existence nor non-existence. If one were to say it has characteristics, why [is it not so] according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*?

The Earth Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva himself said that he cannot be seen; if one claims he is signless (*animitta*), why is it that the great assembly at this gathering is all able to look up and behold the transformation Buddhas upon the light of his crown?
If one claims he possesses both signs and no signs, it ultimately results in contradiction.
If one claims he has neither signs nor no signs, it merely increases frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). The nature of the Tathāgata-garbha is likewise so.
This sutra states that all things are merely objects and there is no such thing as "seeing.
It further states that the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind, which is neither mind nor emptiness, and so forth, up to neither self nor purity;

this is a metaphor for how the Buddha-peak cannot be seen through external forms. The sutra also says that within these myriad phenomena, when one subtly illuminates them, there is nothing that is not seeing.
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgatagarbha—the primordial luminosity of the mind, the wondrous—“is the mind itself, is emptiness,” and so forth, even “is the self and is purity.
This is illustrated by the *Buddhapiṭaka* (Buddha-Topknot), which cannot be perceived through non-characteristics (*animitta*). As the Sūtra says:
“The seer, the conditions for seeing, and the perceived characteristics are like flowers in the sky; they have never existed at all. It further states: “And the Tathāgatagarbha...”

The wondrously luminous mind-source is free from both identity and difference; this is illustrated by the metaphor that the Buddha’s crown cannot be perceived through the characteristics of "both being and non-being.
The Sūtra says: "This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the essence of bodhi—wondrous, pure, and luminous.
How could there be 'is' or 'is not' within it? It further states: "And the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrously luminous mind-source, is..."
This "is not" means that this very thing is like the Buddha’s crown protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*), which cannot be seen through the characteristics of neither existence nor non-existence.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "If one sees all marks as no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. An ancient said: "If one sees all marks as no-marks, then one does not see the Tathāgata.
And it was also said: "If one sees all marks as no-marks, then one sees the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-treasure between the eyebrows)."
The hair grows above the eyes. Furthermore, a verse from the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:
"If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. I have translated this verse as:
"If one abandons seeing me through form, or abandons seeking me through sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata," and so forth. It is also thus.
Furthermore, to be neither identical nor distinct equally constitutes a deviant path;
yet if skillfully employed, these four propositions become four gates, and through each gate one may enter the Way. Therefore, the Buddha’s crown is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgatagarbha.

One must know that whether it be the metaphor or the dharma, there is nothing that is not perfectly free from the four types of false speech. Only when it is perfectly endowed with the four gates is it faultless. This is merely a matter of perspective.
The extensive explanation of the Buddha-dharma is concluded.
Third, regarding the explanation by way of analogy with the dharmas of sentient beings: Now, the nature of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa is inherently present within all living beings;

although delusion and awakening differ as vastly as heaven and abyss, its essence and function are entirely equal. Therefore, one must address the three obstacles currently manifest before sentient beings.
Pointing out the three virtues to let it be known that even if Yan-ruo has not ceased his madness, his head was never lost. As for the three obstructions:

first, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which refers to the delusions of views and thoughts, the delusions of the sands of phenomena, and the delusions of ignorance, which obstruct the three types of bodhi.

Second, the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), which refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or immovable—as well as the partially true uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma that leads to rebirth. Third, the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), which refers to the various forms of suffering resulting from these causes.
The three obstacles to supernatural powers—neither outflowing nor non-outflowing—are the three liberations;

the two obstacles to retribution are the retribution of the shared stage of segmented birth (*bhūta-khaṇḍa*) and the retribution of the transformative birth of the stage of skillful means (*upāya-vaivartika*). The obstacles to the three *nirvāṇas* are as follows:
since the three delusions are themselves the three *bodhi*, why is this so? Because apart from the nature of *bodhi*, there are no separate delusions. As it is said:
Apart from the eyes, there is no staring; the three karmas are themselves the three liberations. Why?
Because apart from the nature of liberation, there are no separate karmas, just as there is no fist apart from the hand. Birth and death in the three lands are themselves nirvāṇa. Why?
Because apart from the nature of nirvāṇa, there is no birth and death, just as there are no flowers apart from empty space. Thus it is said: delusion is itself prajñā, and karma is...
Liberation from suffering is the *dharmakāya*; it is also said that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is *nirvāṇa*, and afflictions (*kleśa*) are *bodhi*.
Question: How do the two phrases and the three phrases relate to one another? Answer: *Bodhi* is ultimate wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*).
When this wisdom illuminates *bodhi*, illuminates liberation, and illuminates *nirvāṇa*, it is called the fruit of *prajñā*.
Nirvāṇa is the ultimate virtue of cessation: it is the cessation of the three delusions, the cessation of the three karmas, and the cessation of birth-and-death within the three lands;
this is called the fruit of liberation. Bodhi is the wisdom of suchness, while Nirvāṇa is the principle of suchness.
The non-duality of wisdom and principle is precisely what is termed the Dharmakāya. As the Sūtra says: "Arising and ceasing are called delusion; the extinction of delusion is called the True."
This is what is called the two designations for the Tathāgata’s supreme enlightenment and great nirvāṇa as the "twofold transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
To clarify this further through a metaphor, the Sūtra says: "Just as water becomes ice, and ice returns to becoming water;

though ice and water seem different in their solidity and flow, their moist nature is the same. This precisely refers to how the nine dharma-realms, following defiled conditions, become deluded regarding their original nature.
The nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* transforms into bodhi, while it transforms into afflictions when nirvāṇa becomes saṃsāra; this is illustrated by the analogy of water turning into ice.
Not only does it lose its appearance of flowing and moistening, but its moist nature itself almost becomes difficult to discern.
Yet, the moist nature has never been absent; since the moist nature remains present, the nature of flowing and moistening likewise has never been absent.

Therefore, when the conditions and the understanding inherent within the nature are removed, it is merely termed the "direct cause" (*dngos rgyu*, *hetu*); yet though it is called the direct cause, it actually possesses both conditions and understanding.

It is only through the Tathāgata’s reliance upon pure conditions that he awakens to the fundamental store-nature (*prakṛti-garbha-dhātu*), transforming afflictions into bodhi and transforming birth-and-death into nirvāṇa.
This is illustrated by the analogy of ice returning to become water; not only is the nature of moisture manifest, but so too is the nature of awakening.
Furthermore, although it circulates and moistens everywhere, even as it circulates and moistens, there is actually no increase in the nature of moisture;

since there is no increase in the nature of moisture, there is likewise no increase in the nature of flowing and moistening. Therefore, all conditions and causes within the cultivation of the Middle Way are in fact only the inherent endowment of nature.
Although we speak of this "inherent endowment," we do not neglect the efficacy of cultivation. One should know that regarding the nine realms...
The seven elements of the nine realms of existence are like ice, while the seven elements of the Buddha-realm are like water; they share the same nature of moisture.
Therefore, the seven elements of the nine realms and the seven elements of the Buddha-realm are both fundamentally pure and pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
For this reason, they are now titled "Great" (*mahā*). The first five [elements] are the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the mind, while the sense organs are...
The "Great" (Mahā) is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind; "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is merely another name for the mind.

Therefore, the seven elements of the nine dharma-realms and the seven elements of the Buddha-realm both belong to the single mind. Since the mind has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*), the title here refers to them as "Buddha.
The seven elements of the nine dharma-realms and the seven elements of the Buddha-realm are both not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because this spontaneity cannot be known through conceptual discrimination or intellectual calculation, it is now titled "The Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
One must not say that while water possesses the meaning of the Great Buddha-Summit, ice does not. Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
"It is like clarifying turbid water; when the mud has been removed and only pure water remains, it is called the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance."

One should know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of birth and death within the nine realms are like turbid water, while the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of the Buddha-realm are like pure clear water.
Although clarity and turbidity differ, their essence and function are identical. Their essence is the same moist nature;
their function is the same flowing and moistening. If one knows that the nature of clear water exists within turbid water, one will certainly not discard the turbid water.

If one seeks pure water elsewhere and encounters turbid water that is nevertheless capable of flowing and moistening, one knows that it is no different from the capacity of pure water to flow and moisten;
thus, there is only a method for clarifying the turbidity, but no separate method for seeking purity.

If, according to this principle, there is no pure water external to turbid water, then it is said that afflictions are themselves bodhi and birth-and-death are themselves nirvana. If, however, [one considers them] separately...
The principle that turbid water must first be clarified means that one transforms afflictions (*kleśa*) into enlightenment (*bodhi*) and transforms birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) into nirvana.
If [the nature] does not exist, how can the meaning of "transformation" be established?

If one does not know that sentient beings are lost in delusion regarding the Great Buddha-Crown Dharma, how could they attain the Great Buddha-Crown Dharma realized by all Buddhas? Therefore, the sutra begins by addressing the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*).

Following the sequential revelation through the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), [the text] universally synthesizes these and subsequently elaborates upon the seven great elements, even fully clarifying that the *tathāgatagarbha* mind is neither identical nor different, neither negated nor illuminated;

it directly reveals that all phenomena—the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind—manifest before all sentient beings are none other than suchness (*dharmatā*). How could this be said to be separate?
How could one seek the essence and function of pure water apart from the essence and function of that turbid water?
If one is unwilling to believe that all sentient beings inherently possess the Great Buddha-Top Dharma, or even if one reverently believes it to be innate yet fails to realize that the afflictions,
karma, and suffering presently manifest are themselves the total essence and total function of the Great Buddha-Top, how then can the wild mind be suddenly stilled?
Cessation is itself Bodhi. For example, one who has originally had no head does not further fear the absence of a head;
likewise, if there were no person who ran madly for fear of losing their head, there would also be no person who realizes the head and whose madness ceases.
Furthermore, regarding the ten causes and six retributions, each and every one is solely the mind. Apart from the mind, they have no substance. Because delusion is great, karma is also great.

Because it is great, suffering is also great; why would this not be the meaning of "Great"? Delusion arises from one's own mind, karma is created by one's own mind, and retribution is experienced by one's own mind;
from beginning to end, cause and effect are never apart from the mind—why would this not be the meaning of "Awakening"?

Delusion has no internal or external essence or characteristics; karma has no accumulated habituation or formal appearance; retribution has no coming, going, or spatial location—why would this not be the meaning of the "Summit"? Furthermore, the ten...

If one must necessarily undergo ten fruits, how can this not be the result of the secret cause? If the six retributions intersect at the six sense organs, how can this not be the principle of mutual functioning?
If a single person is filled and many people are also filled, how can this not be evidence of horizontal pervasiveness?

If this realm reaches the end of the kalpa and one transfers to another realm, how can this not be the proof of vertical exhaustion? If it is thus for the hells, what need is there to mention the other destinies?
Because it can be known, one knows that the twelve classes of beings within the twenty-five states of existence— whether ascending or sinking across the seven realms,
whether spiritual or insentient, whether good or evil, whether joyful or suffering— are each and every one the unchanging nature of the Great Buddha’s Crown.
Taking the entire essence to follow conditions, even at the very moment they are following conditions, each and every one of them...
This refers to the entire substance of the Great Buddha-Crown Nature, which remains unchanging from beginning to end. As the Sūtra says:

"Within this wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action, all are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally without attachment. The "sky" is a metaphor for the unchanging *tathāgatagarbha* (the storehouse consciousness), while the "flowers" are a metaphor for [the mind] following conditions through the seven realms of rebirth.
Since the entirety of the sky is the flowers and the entirety of the flowers is the sky, how could one say that the flowers come and the sky goes?

Is it not that when the flower ceases, the emptiness arises? If this is so for the six classes of ordinary beings, it may likewise be understood for the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings.
Although they do not penetrate the nature of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa, they falsely grasp at partial truth, illusory existence, and the "but-middling" (zhànzhōng) as their ultimate goal;
yet how could the nature of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa ever be altered or changed by those of the three vehicles?

If one were to divide [this reality] and establish that it is not the power of the Great Buddha-Usnīsa-nature—which is the undifferentiated whole that accords with conditions—where else could there be a "partial truth," a "phantasmal existence," or a "middle way" to be grasped? It is like a mani-jewel:
though a fool, ignorant of its use, might trade it for a single garment or a single meal, the essence of the jewel has never been diminished. It is also like the solar disc appearing...

When the light of space enters through a single crack, it is not because the entire sun has entered; yet, when the light from the crack is dim, those who are ignorant observe that crack-light and doubt the sun.
Similarly, those of small wisdom rely on the light from a crack to infer the entirety of the solar disk.
It is likewise with the complete principle of the Great Buddha-Crown possessed by all sentient beings within the nine realms: this dharma of sentient beings is itself [the Great Buddha-Crown].
The mental phenomena do not exist apart from the mind as a separate sentient being, nor does the Buddha-dharma exist apart from the Buddha-dharma as a sentient being,
nor does the Buddha-dharma exist apart from the phenomena of sentient beings. Therefore, within the phenomena of a single sentient being,
one can fully perceive all phenomena of sentient beings, all Buddha-dharmas, and all mental phenomena, none of which are otherwise.
One who possesses the Dharma of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is able, within a single Buddha-dharma, to fully perceive all Buddha-dharmas, all mind-dharmas,
and all sentient-being dharmas as being none other than the Dharma of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; and is also able, within all dharmas,
to fully perceive all mind-dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas, and all sentient-being dharmas as being none other than [the Dharma of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa].
This is what is meant by "skillfully knowing that the Buddha, sentient beings, and the mind are non-differentiated.
One who can read this sutra together with others will not incur the reproach of being a "counting of treasures" nor fall into the calamity of being "unlearned.
The explanation of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is concluded.
Next, the explanation of the *Tathāgataguhyaka-siddhi-niṣṭhārtha* is divided into two parts: first, an analytical explanation, and second, a synthetic explanation.

The analytical explanation consists of four sections: first, explaining "Tathāgata"; second, explaining "secret cause"; third, explaining "cultivation and realization"; and fourth, explaining "definitive meaning.
Regarding the first, the explanation of "Tathāgata," the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "He comes from nowhere, nor does he go anywhere..."
Because it has departed, it is called the Tathāgata. This sutra states that arising and ceasing, departing and arriving, are fundamentally within the true, eternal nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
when one seeks departure, arrival, delusion, awakening, birth, or death therein, nothing at all can be found. All of this is explained in reference to the Dharmakāya.

The *Dharmacakra-pravartana Sūtra* states that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is called "Tathā" and perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) is called "Āgata. This sutra explains [this] as "illumination" (vidyā).

The term "Ultimate" (*parama*) refers to the Tathāgata; both are explained in terms of the *saṃbhogakāya*. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Riding upon the path of reality (*yathābhūta-mārga*), one comes to achieve perfect enlightenment.
This sutra states: "Having perfected self-awakening, one is able to awaken others. Both of these refer to the Tathāgata appearing in the world; they are explained in terms of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Furthermore, ultimate truth (*tattva-satya*) constitutes the path of reality, while all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) constitutes perfect enlightenment.
To sever the afflictions of views and thoughts for oneself is self-awakening; to cause others to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts is awakening others.

This refers to the Tathāgatas of the *śrāvaka* (Tripitaka) and *pratyekabuddha* (Shared) vehicles. To take the Middle Truth as the Path of Suchness and the Knowledge of All Modes as Right Awakening, while severing ignorance for oneself and causing others to sever ignorance, refers to the Tathāgatas of the Distinct and Perfect vehicles. Furthermore, [this] brings forth the Two Truths.
Externally, the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is non-discrimination between the two extremes; this is called Right Enlightenment.

By severing the twelve grades of ignorance, one reaches the ultimate limit of clarity—this is the distinct teaching of the Tathāgata. Internally, the primary truth is the single mind with its threefold wisdom;
this is called Right Enlightenment. By exhausting the forty-two grades of ignorance, one reaches the ultimate limit of clarity.

The Tathāgata of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): Furthermore, the Dharmakāya is inherently present, the Sambhogakāya is accomplished through cultivation, and the Nirmāṇakāya arises in function—this is the Tathāgata of the Separate Teaching (Biejiao).

That all three bodies are entirely inherent in nature (*xingju*) and also entirely manifest through cultivation, such that nature and cultivation are non-dual, is the Tathāgata of the Perfect Teaching.
Here, we specifically refer to the Tathāgata of the Perfect Teaching, who represents the ultimate consummation of cultivated virtue.
This is the ultimate fruit that accords with the nature itself. Next, regarding the explanation of the "mysterious cause" (*mi-yin*):

taking non-arising and non-ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, one subsequently achieves the perfect realization of the ground of fruition. Because the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition and the fruition penetrates the source of the cause, it is called "mysterious.

Furthermore, the correct cause of Buddha-nature (*zheng-yin foxing*), the conditional cause of Buddha-nature (*yuan-yin foxing*), and the penetrating cause of Buddha-nature (*liao-yin foxing*) are all perfectly complete.
Because cultivation is perfected such that it is neither sequential nor simultaneous, neither unified nor distinct, it is called "Esoteric" (*mi*). Furthermore, a sutra says:
"Although you possess a powerful memory, this merely increases your erudition; regarding *śamatha*, your mind has not yet realized its subtle and esoteric contemplation.
It further says: "All these various stages are observed with the diamond-like [wisdom] through the ten profound parables of the illusory nature."
Within *śamatha*, one employs the various Tathāgatas; through the purification and realization of *vipaśyanā*, one gradually enters deeper.
Now, *śamatha* is the threefold cessation within a single mind, and *vipaśyanā* is the threefold contemplation within a single mind.
That which is the subtle and secret contemplative illumination of *śamatha* is the non-duality of cessation and contemplation; it arises from the perfect realm of truth (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*).
Perfect Śamatha and Vipaśyanā illuminate the Perfect Realm; because there is no wisdom outside of Suchness and no Suchness outside of wisdom, it is called "mysterious.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the sutra, Ānanda, seeing the Buddha, earnestly requested the initial expedient means by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained the wondrous Śamatha, Samādhi, and Dhyāna of Bodhi—this was his question.

This esoteric cause consists of three virtues that are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor distinct—like the world’s letter *tryaṃbaka* (the three-eyed mark) or the three eyes of a deity;
this is what is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*). The wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* you have asked about are likewise so:
*śamatha* is the cessation that realizes reality, and it is also the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); *samādhi*... [is the contemplation of the marvelous existence].
This "convenience" (upāya) is the cessation that accords with conditions (*anupaśama*), which is also the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-darśana*);

"samādhi" is the cessation that quiets the discrimination of the two extremes (*antadvaya-vikalpa*), which is also the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-darśana*). Furthermore, *śamatha* is the single mind of the three cessations; *samādhi* is the single mind of the three contemplations;
and *dhyāna* is the non-duality of cessation and contemplation. If they were fixed as three, they would not be called the "wondrous three"; if they were fixed as one...
One is not called "wondrous" [if it is merely one]; rather, it is neither one nor three, yet it is three and one. That which is one is eternally three, and that which is three is eternally one.
Only when one and three are inconceivable can they be called "wondrous. This wondrousness is itself the Esoteric (Mitsu).
Furthermore, at the beginning of the Sūtra, in response to Ānanda’s request, the Buddha first declares: "There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown (Mahā-uṣṇīṣa)."

The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the king of sūtras, is fully endowed with the myriad practices; it is the path of wondrous adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend by a single gate.
It subsequently refutes that the reflected image of conditions is not the mind, revealing the true mark of the nature of seeing.

It synthesizes the four categories to return to principle and clarifies that the seven elements are intrinsically complete. Finally, it culminates in the *tathāgatagarbha* mind, wherein [all phenomena] are neither identical nor different.
It simultaneously negates and illuminates, without a single word being spoken regarding the methods for practicing this samādhi;

it merely reveals the principle of the perfect and wondrous Three Truths of our own original nature. One should know that when this rational nature is realized, wondrous practice is spontaneously perfected—because the entirety of nature gives rise to practice, and the entirety of practice resides within nature;
therefore, it is called "Esoteric. Furthermore, this is the Perfect and Sudden Calm Abiding.
Contemplating this as the cause for attaining Buddhahood, the nature of the Great Buddha-Crown (Mahā-uṣṇīṣa) is also the cause of the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*;
thus it is called the "cause of the cause. The unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Tathāgata is the fruit of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Because this "fruit of the fruit" serves as the "cause of the cause," the principle of cause and effect is subtle and inconceivable; therefore, it is termed "esoteric" (*guhya*). Third, the explanation of cultivation and realization.

Regarding the cultivation of the conditioned (*sopadhika-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of the ultimate truth (*tattva-bhāvanā*): there is the stage of partial realization (*bhāga-prativedha*), the stage of full realization (*paripūrṇa-prativedha*), and so forth.

If one says that in the stages of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri nirvedhabhāgīyāni*), the factors of the path (*mārga-dharma*) are cultivated as the condition for the truth (*tattva-ālambana-bhāvanā*), and that after having seen the truths (*satya-darśana*), the subsequent repeated contemplation (*paryeṣaṇā*) takes the truth as its object and is thus "cultivation of the truth"—this is the intent of the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) teachings.

If one says that in the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi*), the wisdom of emptiness resembling the non-arising (*anutpāda-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is cultivated as the condition for seeing the ground (*darśana-bhūmi*)—this is the intent of the *Mahāyāna*.
To say that subsequently, true wisdom of non-arising is "true cultivation" (zhenxiu) represents the intent of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
